claims.text: Wear performance in HEA protective coatings is governed by microstructural evolution induced by compositional modification.
Increasing the concentration of an oxide-forming element increases lattice distortion in an HEA coating.
Greater lattice distortion enhances coating hardness.
Greater lattice distortion enhances coating toughness.
Increasing the concentration of an oxide-forming element promotes formation of a uniform, adherent, nanometer-scale oxide layer during wear.
The combination of increased lattice distortion and a protective oxide layer reduces wear rate.
The as-deposited coatings contain multiple principal elements in a stable phase.
Increasing the oxide-forming element concentration drives formation of a protective oxide scale during wear.
Enhanced hardness reduces plastic deformation and material removal during sliding.
The oxide layer acts as a barrier that reduces plastic deformation and material removal during sliding.
Coatings with more oxide-forming element will have lower wear rates than baseline coatings.
Coatings with more oxide-forming element will have higher hardness than baseline coatings.
Coatings with more oxide-forming element will develop a more continuous and protective oxide tribolayer than baseline coatings.
Baseline coatings with less oxide-forming element develop a less uniform or thinner oxide scale.
Baseline coatings with less oxide-forming element have lower hardness under identical conditions.
The proposed relationship holds only over composition ranges that maintain alloy stability.
The proposed relationship holds under moderate wear conditions that permit beneficial oxide formation without detrimental phase changes.
